author: product-requirements-expert
title: Specialty directory
summary: One page lists every specialty the clinic knows, under its stored name, each with the veterinarians holding it shown by full name. Read-only, no pagination, reached by its own address alone.
acceptance_criteria: Opening the specialty directory lists every specialty the clinic knows, once each, under its stored name, on a single page with no pagination.
A specialty held by veterinarians shows every holder by first name then last name, for example "Helen Leary".
A specialty no veterinarian holds is still listed, and is shown as held by none rather than left blank.
A veterinarian holding no specialty appears nowhere on the page.
A veterinarian holding more than one specialty appears under each of them.
The page offers no way to add, change, or remove a specialty or a veterinarian; NG-2 is unchanged.
No other page of the system links to the specialty directory, and no navigation entry is added for it.
The page carries the same navigation as every other page, as REQ-SYS-001 requires.
Specialties are listed in a stable order, and so are the veterinarians within each specialty.
When the clinic knows no specialties at all, the page opens and reports that there are none rather than failing.

Per REQ-LANG-002, no user-facing wording the page introduces is hard-coded, and every new piece of wording is present in all eleven supported languages. Stored specialty names are data and are shown as stored.
non_goals: Managing veterinarians or specialties through the application (NG-2, unchanged)
A navigation entry or a link to the page from anywhere else
A machine-readable form of the specialty list
Searching or filtering the specialty list (NG-9)
notes: Owner-stated address for the page: GET /specialties.html (dispatch, 2026-08-10); the route contract belongs in system-design.md#contracts. This requirement was stated by the owner, not derived from code like the rest of this PRD. file_targets are best-effort; the template path and whether a new controller is warranted are design calls. Two open questions are recorded in docs/prd.md rather than consulted, per the dispatch: which order the listing uses (only stability is required), and whether a visible entry point follows later. Non-Goals table unchanged, so no scope_overrides.

author: system-design-expert
architectural_fit: One slice, no split: the page is a single behavior, and its wording is part of that behavior rather than an independent one. Every pattern it needs is already In force in architecture-principles.md, but the slice is new ground on three counts recorded in docs/system-design.md#contracts: a new HTTP surface, the first repository over Specialty, and the first view-assembly value type in this codebase. It stays inside the vet feature package (ADR 2026-07-31-feature-package-organization) and inside server-side rendering (ADR 2026-07-31-server-side-rendering-with-thymeleaf); owner and system are untouched, so the acyclic package graph holds. No ADR: nothing here departs from the catalog, and no reasonable alternative is being rejected. The PRD's file_targets are superseded on two entries, as its notes anticipated. VetController is not extended and VetRepository gains no method; the route is a different HTTP surface and Specialty is a different entity, so a new SpecialtyController and a new SpecialtyRepository carry them. VetRepository.findAll() is reused unchanged for the veterinarian side. Basis for the fit claims is grep plus direct reads of the vet package and CacheConfiguration; the IDE oracle is not connected on this run, so treat the symbol claims as the weaker basis.
integration_points: GET /specialties.html is the page's only address; it takes no request parameter, since there is no paging (NG) and no filtering (NG-9). The path is recorded once, in the SpecialtyController row of docs/system-design.md#contracts.
SpecialtyRepository reads the existing specialties table; VetRepository.findAll() supplies the veterinarian side. No schema change, no data.sql change, no new dependency.

The page renders through fragments/layout.html like every other page, so REQ-SYS-001 navigation comes for free. The layout's menu argument selects the active nav item by string match: pass a value matching no existing item so nothing is highlighted, which is how 'no navigation entry, no inbound link' is honored while still carrying the shared nav. layout.html itself is not edited.

messages.properties gains new keys, and I18nPropertiesSyncTest.checkI18nPropertyFilesAreInSync then requires each one in the nine translated bundles (de, es, fa, hi, ja, ko, pt, ru, tr). messages_en.properties is deliberately empty and is skipped by that test; English resolves from the base bundle. That is the eleventh language, already satisfied.
CacheConfiguration is not touched: the specialty read is uncached, so no new JCache cache is declared.

patterns.description: The precedent for a repository over a lookup entity with an explicit name-ordered query. Follow it for the ordering, but declare SpecialtyRepository as extends Repository<Specialty, Integer> with only the read method, matching VetRepository's narrow surface rather than PetTypeRepository's JpaRepository. NG-2 keeps this read-only, and a full CRUD surface would contradict that.

The controller shape to copy: package-private, constructor-injected repositories, a @GetMapping returning a view name, model attributes added and nothing else. SpecialtyController binds the request, calls the two repositories, calls SpecialtyDirectory, and selects the view.

Pattern Catalog, Web controller row plus the Design Validation Checklist line 'No business rule added to a web controller'. The existing controller-held-rules deviation explicitly does not extend to new rules, so the fold lives in SpecialtyDirectory: an immutable value type in the vet package with a static factory over the two collections, unit-testable with real objects and no Spring context. Entry rows expose a specialty and its holders.

The template idiom to follow, including the existing #{none} wording for a veterinarian holding no specialty. Reuse it for a specialty held by none. Reuse #{specialties}, #{vets}, and #{name} too: only the page-level empty state ('the clinic knows no specialties') is wording no bundle carries yet, so the new-key footprint is one key, not a page's worth.

risks.risk: Specialty and Vet inherit from BaseEntity, which overrides neither equals nor hashCode. Under @WebMvcTest with a mocked repository, the Specialty instances returned by the specialty read and those hanging off each Vet are distinct objects, so a fold that matches by object equality silently reports every specialty as held by none — and passes under a persistence context where the instances happen to be shared.
risks.mitigation: Match holders to specialties by getId(). Write the SpecialtyDirectory test with independently constructed Specialty instances carrying equal ids, so the test fails against reference matching.

risks.risk: Annotating the specialty read @Cacheable("vets") to mirror VetRepository would collide: the vets cache already holds VetRepository.findAll()'s no-argument entry under the same empty key, and a second no-argument method would read a Collection<Vet> back as a Collection<Specialty> and throw ClassCastException at runtime, not at compile time.
risks.mitigation: Leave SpecialtyRepository uncached. If caching is ever wanted, it needs its own cache name declared in CacheConfiguration, and Open Question 5 (no eviction is configured for vets) applies to it too.

risks.risk: The veterinarian side comes from the cached VetRepository.findAll(), so the directory inherits the vet cache's staleness. This is the known Open Question 5, not a new defect, but it means the directory and the vet list can only ever agree with each other, not necessarily with the database.
risks.mitigation: Accept and leave unchanged; do not add eviction as part of this slice.

risks.risk: I18nPropertiesSyncTest.checkNonInternationalizedStrings scans every .html under src/main and fails on any line carrying literal text between tags without a message expression or a th:text attribute on the same line. A prototype-text template written in the usual style trips it if the th:text lands on a different line.
risks.mitigation: Keep each literal-bearing element's th:text on the same line as its text, as vetList.html does. Run ./gradlew test before assuming the page is done; this test is the enforcement point for REQ-LANG-002 and has no contract row.

risks.risk: Stored specialty names are data. Translating them, or routing them through a message key, would break the acceptance criterion that they are shown as stored.
risks.mitigation: Render them with th:text on the value, never th:utext and never a message lookup. th:text also keeps Thymeleaf's escaping on, which is the only XSS control this page has.

risks.risk: Vet.specialties is mapped EAGER and spring.jpa.open-in-view is disabled. A fold that leans on lazy loading during view rendering would throw. This is safe as mapped today, but only because the fold materializes everything before the view runs.
risks.mitigation: Do the whole fold in SpecialtyDirectory before returning from the controller. Do not pass repository results or streams into the model.

notes: Verdict rationale for the record: covered fails because no read path to Specialty exists and the page is a new HTTP surface; minor fails because three new types and a new route are more than an adjustment; refactor-first fails because nothing must be reshaped first — the existing abstractions accommodate the slice as they stand. || docs/system-design.md is updated: the Contracts table gains SpecialtyRepository, SpecialtyDirectory, and SpecialtyController rows carrying Implements REQ-SPEC-001, and the 'Invariants the rows cannot carry' paragraph records that the directory is assembled outside its controller with a fixed order. The provenance banner now scopes its derived-from-code claim, and post-survey design statements are marked (designed) until the code lands. doc-sync drops those marks once the slice is implemented. || Ordering: specialties by name in the JPQL query, following PetTypeRepository.findPetTypes(). Holders by last name then first name, sorted inside SpecialtyDirectory. VetRepository.findAll() returns a Collection whose order is database-dependent — do not rely on it. Only stability is required by the PRD, so name order is a design choice, not a requirement; the PRD's first open question stays open and is not resolved here. || Test placement follows testing-principles: the fold behaviors (every specialty listed once, a specialty held by none, a veterinarian with no specialty omitted, a veterinarian under each of several specialties) belong in SpecialtyDirectoryTests as plain unit tests over real Vet and Specialty objects, with no Spring context and no Mockito. SpecialtyControllerTests keeps the MockMvc slice: route resolves, view name, model attribute, full-name rendering, and the empty-state wording. Keep the five PRD test names; add one for the multi-specialty criterion in the same BDD style. || Naming: 'directory' comes from the PRD title and names a page, not a domain concept. Specialty and Veterinarian remain the canonical terms per docs/ubiquitous-language.md, and 'Vet' stays the accepted short form in code. No new domain term is introduced, so ubiquitous-language.md is unchanged; adding one is product-requirements-expert's call, not this slice's. || Security: no new trust boundary. The route is an unparameterized read-only GET, so there is no input to validate, no identifier to tamper with, and no secret in play. It is open to every caller like every other route — the posture recorded in docs/system-design.md#security-context, unchanged by this slice. The one control that matters is Thymeleaf's default escaping of the stored specialty and veterinarian names. || Reliability: the two reads are unpaged. The seeded specialties table holds three rows and the vets table six, so no resource limit is warranted now; a specialty table that grew unbounded would need paging, and the PRD rules paging out for this slice. The only failure mode is a data-access failure, which propagates to the existing error page. || Residual open question, recorded not consulted: the seed data holds no unheld specialty, so the held-by-none path has no integration-level fixture and is exercised only at the unit and MockMvc levels. || Observation, not part of this slice: the Implementation Order table in docs/system-design.md is still empty behind a comment saying it is populated once the PRD defines requirements. The PRD now does. Filling it needs the whole requirement dependency graph and is a doc-sync or PRD-side job, not this slice's.

author: security-reviewer
approved_aspects: No injection surface added: SpecialtyRepository.findSpecialties() is a static, parameterless JPQL string (SELECT specialty FROM Specialty specialty ORDER BY specialty.name) with no concatenation and no nativeQuery; SpecialtyController takes no request parameters, path variables, or form binding, so no attacker-controlled value reaches the data access layer.

Output escaping holds: specialtyList.html renders every dynamic value through th:text (specialty name, holder first/last name) with Thymeleaf's default escaping intact. Swept the whole new template for the unescaped-output class - no th:utext, no [[...]] inlining, no th:attr sink carrying model data. Consistent with the existing vetList.html pattern and with the system-design Threat Model row on cross-site scripting.

Data exposure weighed and judged not a new disclosure: /specialties.html publishes veterinarian full names grouped by specialty, which is the same data set already served unauthenticated at /vets.html (HTML) and /vets (serialized). The slice re-projects public data rather than exposing a new PII class, so it introduces no new row in the system-design Threat Model. The absent navigation entry is a product decision (PRD open question), not a security control - it is not obscurity being relied on, since the underlying data is already linked and reachable.

No new authentication or authorization boundary is crossed: the endpoint is read-only GET with no mutating path, and it inherits the project-wide no-auth posture already recorded in system-design Security Context. The design's read-only intent is enforced structurally - SpecialtyRepository extends the bare Repository marker and declares only @Transactional(readOnly = true) reads, exposing no save or delete.
Supply chain unchanged: build.gradle, settings.gradle, and gradle/ carry no diff, so no dependency was added, upgraded, or repinned and no new CVE surface enters with this slice.

No secrets introduced: swept the full change set for credential-shaped material (password, secret, token, api key, credential) and for dangerous execution or deserialization sinks (Runtime.exec, ProcessBuilder, readObject, createQuery, nativeQuery, string-concatenated queries) - zero hits. The ten message-bundle additions are a single plain-text noSpecialties value per locale, rendered through an escaped th:text.

Model exposure is bounded: the controller publishes a SpecialtyDirectory value type built before rendering, with defensive List.copyOf in both record constructors, so the view holds no repository handle and no lazily loaded association that could widen what the page reads.

author: test-reviewer

findings.description: The input list List.of(dentistry, radiology, surgery) is already in alphabetical order, and the assertion checks the same order back out. This cannot distinguish 'SpecialtyDirectory.of preserves the given order' (the documented contract: 'in the order the specialties were given') from 'SpecialtyDirectory.of resorts by name' — a regression that added an internal sort would still pass this test. theSpecialtyDirectoryShouldOrderHoldersByLastNameThenFirstName already uses a non-alphabetical input (Sharon, Zack, Amy) specifically so the assertion has discriminating power; this test should do the same for the specialty-level order, e.g. List.of(surgery, dentistry, radiology) asserted back in that order.
findings.fix: Reorder the input specialties to a non-alphabetical sequence (e.g. surgery, dentistry, radiology) and assert entries come back in that same given order, so the test actually exercises order preservation rather than coinciding with alphabetical sort.

findings.description: SpecialtyRepository.findSpecialties() — the slice's one new persistence query, including its 'ORDER BY specialty.name' clause — has no integration-level test exercising it against a real database. Both new test classes construct Specialty/Vet objects directly and never touch the repository. The design-block named PetTypeRepository.findPetTypes() as this repository's precedent, and that method is exercised by ClinicServiceTests (@DataJpaTest, real seeded H2 data, asserting name order) — SpecialtyRepository has no equivalent. A typo in the JPQL, wrong ordering column, or wrong entity mapping would pass every currently-existing test.
findings.fix: Add a @DataJpaTest case exercising SpecialtyRepository.findSpecialties() against the seeded data (ClinicServiceTests already wires @DataJpaTest with PetTypeRepository as the pattern to copy for a lookup-entity repository), asserting the seeded specialties come back in name order.

approved_aspects: Unit/MockMvc split matches testing-principles' pyramid guidance: fold behavior lives in plain-object SpecialtyDirectoryTests with no Spring context, HTTP/view concerns stay in the MockMvc slice — no logic duplicated between the two layers.

createVetHolding's deliberate per-vet Specialty copies (SpecialtyDirectoryTests) are a real regression guard for BaseEntity's missing equals/hashCode, with a javadoc that explains why rather than narrating what — confirmed by reading SpecialtyDirectory.of, which matches holders to specialties by getId(), not object identity.
BDD test names throughout (the{Subject}Should{Outcome}) read as specifications and match the PRD's test_names list plus one justified addition for the multi-specialty criterion.
Four-phase structure held cleanly (blank-line-separated arrange/act/assert, no phase comments) in every test read.
Three-tier data naming observed: RADIOLOGY_ID/SURGERY_ID/DENTISTRY_ID name meaningful values by role; no bare mystery literals.

AssertJ used fluently throughout (extracting/tuple/flatExtracting); MockMvc's content().string(containsString(...)) is the correct idiom for that API and is not a violation of the no-JUnit-assertEquals rule.

On the implementer's flagged trade-off (asserting the rendered English 'There are no specialties on record' vs. an id-based selector): the content-string assertion is judged acceptable. It verifies the actual behavior an acceptance criterion names ('reports that there are none rather than failing') at the one layer that renders it, is internally consistent with the file's other three content assertions including the sibling '>none<' check, and no existing controller test in this codebase establishes a competing convention to prefer. The trade-off is real (a wording-only edit to the base bundle breaks this test), but content assertions on rendered MockMvc output are an accepted pattern here and the alternative (an id/CSS selector) would only prove an empty block rendered, not that the required message text is present.

New classes carry 100% line coverage per jacocoTestReport (SpecialtyDirectory, SpecialtyDirectory.Entry, SpecialtyController, Specialty), exceeding the 80% domain-package target in testing-principles.md.

author: test-reviewer
approved_aspects: Finding 1 resolved: theSpecialtyDirectoryShouldListEverySpecialtyOnOnePage now feeds List.of(surgery, dentistry, radiology) — a non-alphabetical input — and asserts containsExactly("surgery", "dentistry", "radiology") back in that same given order, giving the assertion real discriminating power against an internal-sort regression, matching the sibling holder-order test's pattern.

Finding 2's substance is resolved, and the Red-check discipline behind it is sound. shouldFindAllSpecialtiesInNameOrder exercises SpecialtyRepository.findSpecialties() against real seeded H2 data via the ClinicServiceTests @DataJpaTest-equivalent harness, following the shouldFindAllPetTypes precedent named in the original finding. It closes the JPQL-validity and entity-mapping gaps the finding raised (a typo or wrong entity mapping now fails this test) and catches an ORDER BY on the wrong column: verified against src/main/resources/db/h2/data.sql, which seeds specialties as (radiology, surgery, dentistry) — not alphabetical — so an ORDER BY id or insertion-order regression would produce a different sequence than the asserted (dentistry, radiology, surgery) and fail.

The one honestly-scoped residual gap — an entirely deleted ORDER BY clause coincidentally still returning name order on this H2 fixture — is empirically grounded, not asserted from theory: the implementer ran the Red check by deleting the clause and observing the test still pass, and cross-checked the schema (src/main/resources/db/h2/schema.sql:21, CREATE INDEX specialties_name ON specialties (name)) as the mechanism. Given the seed order is not already alphabetical, this is a real, non-obvious H2 optimizer behavior rather than a coincidence of insertion order, so the empirical claim is credible.

The javadoc replacing the comment states the limit plainly and accurately: it says the order assertion is 'the weaker half of that guard against H2 specifically' for the lost-ORDER-BY case, without overclaiming general ORDER BY coverage. This is the right resolution under tested-as-spec — restoring production code unchanged (correct, since the test cannot force a Red state here) and documenting the honest limit beats deleting a test that still earns its keep on JPQL validity, entity mapping, and wrong-column ordering.

Re-ran the two affected test classes (SpecialtyDirectoryTests, ClinicServiceTests) via ./gradlew test — both pass cleanly, and production code (SpecialtyRepository.java) is byte-identical to the version already reviewed and approved by security-reviewer and code-quality-reviewer.

author: doc-reviewer

findings.description: The javadoc claims the order assertion is 'the weaker half of that guard against H2 specifically' because 'a query that lost its ORDER BY would read through that index and return the same sequence anyway.' This is inaccurate: the seed data (src/main/resources/db/h2/data.sql) inserts specialties as radiology, surgery, dentistry — not name order. A plain SELECT with no ORDER BY has no defined row order and, absent a predicate on the indexed column, typically returns rows in table/insertion order rather than via the secondary index, i.e. radiology, surgery, dentistry — which would fail the containsExactly("dentistry", "radiology", "surgery") assertion. The comment tells a future reader the ORDER BY clause is unguarded by this test, when the non-alphabetical seed order means it actually is guarded. Left uncorrected, this misleads maintainers about what regression protection exists here.
findings.fix: Exercises the specialty query against the seeded schema: JPQL validity, entity * mapping, and the name order the directory page depends on. The seed data inserts * specialties as radiology, surgery, dentistry — not name order — so this assertion * fails if the query's ORDER BY clause is lost or wrong.

approved_aspects: The other test-reviewer autofix (SpecialtyDirectoryTests.theSpecialtyDirectoryShouldListEverySpecialtyOnOnePage) is correctly applied: input specialties are now given in the non-alphabetical order surgery, dentistry, radiology and asserted back in that same order, giving the assertion real discriminating power against an internal re-sort — matches the pattern already used by theSpecialtyDirectoryShouldOrderHoldersByLastNameThenFirstName.

shouldFindAllSpecialtiesInNameOrder correctly closes the integration-test gap the test-reviewer identified: it exercises SpecialtyRepository.findSpecialties() through @DataJpaTest against real seeded H2 data, following the ClinicServiceTests/PetTypeRepository precedent named in the design-block.

No docs/ changes in this delta (confirmed via scripts/changeset.sh and the handoff timeline); docs/prd.md and docs/system-design.md content approved in the prior review round still matches the landed code — no re-review needed for those files.
No new PRD-boundary, cross-document coherence, or structural issues introduced by this delta.
